newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sueno collapse likely to affect Japan banking--MOF.
newsitem.headline: Sueno collapse likely to affect Japan banking--MOF.

text.p: Japan's financial institutions will likely be affected by the potential collapse of realtor Sueno Kosan, Finance Minister Wataru Kubo told a news conference on Tuesday.

Earlier on Tuesday, the Housing Loan Administration Corp (HLAC), a body set up to collect problem loans run up by Japan's failed "jusen" mortgage firms, said it had asked an Osaka court to declare realtor Sueno Kosan bankrupt.
Kubo said non-bank financial institutions which made loans to Sueno may not be able to recover all their lending, so the creditors of these non-bank institutions are also likely to be affected.
"However, such an impact will be resolved among related financial institutions in accordance with our financial system," he said.

Kubo also said the HLAC's request that Sueno be declared bankrupt was necessary in order to preserve the company's assets. Earlier this year, Sueno Kosan chief Kenichi Sueno pleaded guilty to charges that he and some aides hid the company's assets to prevent them being seized by creditors.
Kubo added that HLAC's request was an important step in the process of recovering mortgage companies' bad loans.

Asked about the impact of non-banks' bad loans on the Japanese financial system, Kubo said it was "a difficult question". He added that it was difficult to say yet how loans to Sueno, other than those by the jusen, would be recovered.

Regarding the World Trade Organisation's (WTO) recent ruling that Japan's liquor taxes are unfair to foreign products, Kubo said Japan was considering what measures to take, and that it would deal with the problem within the framework of the WTO.
"This was a very severe ruling for us and it is very regrettable. However, we must work within the framework as a member of the WTO," he said.
He declined to comment on whether Japan would revise its liquor taxes in its annual tax reviews for next fiscal year beginning April 1.
Kubo said Japan was unlikely to put forward any details on how it plans to deal with the ruling at the next WTO meeting on liquor taxes scheduled for November 20.
